foods.name: Kabocha squash

ageBands.prepMd:
Steam or roast until completely soft, then cut into finger-length wedges about
two fingers thick. Remove the skin for a beginner — kabocha skin stays chewy
even when the flesh is soft, and chewy is the harder texture.
Soft cubes around thumbnail size once the pincer grasp arrives.

Serve it the way the rest of the table eats it — cubed in a soup, mashed as a
side, or roasted in wedges. Skin can stay on now if it's roasted soft.

choking.requiredModification: Steam or roast until a fork meets no resistance; skin removed for beginners.

foods.backgroundMd:
Dense, sweet winter squash — 단호박 in Korean, where it's a common early
weaning food, often steamed and mashed thin. Behaves almost identically to
[[sweet-potato]] once cooked, so it's a natural second food if the first went
well: same shapes, same softness test, different flavour.
foods.safetyNoteMd:
The raw squash is very hard and needs real force to cut — that firmness is
exactly the hazard, so the softness test matters more here than with a
softer-fleshed vegetable. Press a cooked piece between thumb and forefinger
before serving; if it holds its shape under pressure, cook it longer.

foods.name: Peanut

ageBands.servingNote: Thinned to the consistency of a runny yoghurt — never a spoonful or a thick glob.
ageBands.prepMd:
Stir about 1/4 teaspoon of smooth peanut butter into warm water, breast milk,
formula, or a puree the baby already eats, until it's thin enough to pour off
a spoon. Offer it in the morning, at home, on a day you're not rushing —
that's a logistics choice, not a medical one: it means you're watching, and
your clinic is open.

Watch for about two hours. IgE reactions happen within minutes to two hours,
which is also why the familiar "wait 3–5 days before the next new food" rule
adds nothing diagnostically — it just slows down variety.

Same thinned form. Thickness, not quantity, is the hazard here: nut butter
stiff enough to hold its shape can obstruct an airway.

Still thinned or spread thinly — on a strip of toast, stirred into oatmeal or
yoghurt. The maintenance target doesn't change: keep it in the rotation at
least three times a week rather than letting weeks lapse.

allergenProtocol.firstDose: About 1/4 tsp of smooth peanut butter thinned with warm water, breast milk, or formula, stirred into a familiar puree.
allergenProtocol.medicalGate: If your baby has severe eczema, an egg allergy, or both, talk to your pediatrician or an allergist BEFORE the first peanut exposure — that group may need testing and a supervised introduction between 4 and 6 months (NIAID 2017 addendum, Tier 1). Most other infants can be introduced at home. Do not ask for a broad allergy panel: in infants without symptoms its positive predictive value is very low, and false positives lead to unnecessary lifelong avoidance.

choking.note: Whole peanuts are a high-risk choking hazard and are not appropriate before age 4.
choking.requiredModification: Never whole nuts and never a spoonful or thick glob of nut butter — thin it, or spread it very thinly.

sources.body: NIAID (Addendum Guidelines for the Prevention of Peanut Allergy, 2017)
CSACI — "early introduction is not enough" position statement

foods.backgroundMd:
The single most consequential food on this list. The LEAP trial randomized
infants at high risk to eat peanut or avoid it, and early, sustained
introduction reduced peanut allergy by roughly 81%. That result is why the
old "delay allergens" advice was reversed.

The part that gets lost: **introduction is not the finish line.** LEAP's
protocol wasn't a taste, it was about 6 g of peanut protein a week across
three or more feedings, sustained for years. CSACI's position statement is
blunt that occasional exposure may be worse than none — a single taste
followed by months of nothing can raise the risk of sensitization rather than
lower it. So this food has a maintenance schedule, not a checkbox.
foods.safetyNoteMd:
Two separate risks, often confused.

**Allergy** is managed by early, regular exposure — with the medical gate
above for babies with severe eczema or egg allergy.

**Choking** is managed by form. Whole peanuts and tree nuts are firm, round,
and airway-sized: AAP keeps them off the list until age 4. A spoonful of thick
peanut butter is on the same list. Thinned or spread very thinly, peanut is
fine from six months.

foods.name: Sweet potato

ageBands.servingNote: Expect more on the face and tray than in the mouth. That is the job at this age.
ageBands.prepMd:
Roast or steam until a fork slides in with no resistance, then cut into
finger-length wedges about as thick as two of your fingers. Leave the skin on
for a beginner — it gives something to grip, and the flesh is what gets eaten.

At this age the palmar grasp means the whole piece is held in the fist with an
end sticking out, so the baby controls the bite. Pieces cut small are actually
*harder* now, not safer: they can't be picked up, and they end up scooped by
the handful.

Once the pincer grasp appears — usually around nine months — switch to soft
cubes roughly the size of your thumbnail. Keep offering a few larger pieces
alongside, since biting and tearing are their own skills worth practising.

Whatever the rest of the table is having — cubed, mashed, or in wedges. Keep
offering some pieces big enough to bite from rather than only pincer-sized
ones; biting and tearing are still skills in progress.

choking.requiredModification: Cook until it smashes easily between thumb and forefinger.

foods.backgroundMd:
A soft, sweet root vegetable that holds its shape when roasted, which makes it
one of the easier first foods to hand over whole. Rich in beta-carotene, and
its vitamin C helps the body absorb non-heme iron from the same meal — worth
pairing with beans, lentils, or fortified cereal.

Related: [[kabocha]] behaves almost identically once cooked.
foods.safetyNoteMd:
Cooked sweet potato is low risk once it mashes with light pressure between two
fingers. Undercooked pieces are firm enough to be a hazard, so test a piece
before serving rather than trusting the timer.

Raw sweet potato is a hard raw vegetable and is not appropriate at any age in
this range.
